A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TCP-Diffusion work, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–D. Supplementary material mentioned but not included in v1 cannot establish what was previously documented outside the supplied PDF.

before.justification: v1 reports original TC rainfall forecasting experiments, comparisons with DL and NWP methods, component ablations, and qualitative predictions in Tables 1–3 and Figures 3–4.

after.justification: v2 retains original forecasting experiments and adds repeated stochastic predictions, runtime comparisons, spectral diagnostics, FuXi comparisons, and cyclone phase and intensity analyses.

M1.justification: The ARP targets, rainfall reconstruction, conditional EA-3DUNet, historical encoders, ResNet-18 forecast encoder, and denoising objective remain unchanged. New pseudocode and expanded input and hyperparameter descriptions document the existing method; they do not establish an implemented algorithm or architecture change.

E1.justification: Both versions use MSWEP, ERA5, and IBTrACS data for the same global TC-centered, 10-degree rainfall forecasting task, covering 1980–2020 and predicting 12 hours at three-hour intervals. The new 2020 subset, phase/intensity breakdowns, and case visualizations remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Persistence, U-Net, PreDiff, and NowcastNet. v2 adds ERA5-IFS alongside ECMWF-IFS in Table 2 and introduces FuXi in Appendix D.6/Table 6. These materially broaden comparisons to the input forecast system itself and a learned global weather model.

E3.justification: The reported main evaluation changes from repeated selections of half the test set to stochastic predictions across the full test set. Added evaluation protocols include RAPSD diagnostics, separate lead-time scores, timing comparisons, and a FuXi comparison using 349 samples from 2020 at 6–12-hour leads. The stated dataset split counts and six-hour NWP alignment remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component ablation remains, while v2 adds substantial analyses of spatial fidelity through RAPSD, lead-time-dependent skill and rainfall distributions, and errors across cyclone lifecycle phases and intensities. Figures 9 and 13 additionally examine eight stochastic predictions and an Olivia case against NWP forecasts.

E5.justification: v1 averages ten random half-test-set evaluations without reporting dispersion. v2 describes eight independent diffusion-noise predictions per test case and reports individual scores, means, and standard deviations in Table 5. This changes the estimation procedure and introduces explicit uncertainty reporting; the eight predictions are inference samples, not separate training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1's TCP-Diffusion ETS-6/24/60 and TPMAE values change from 0.43766/0.14971/0.00742/0.42582 to 0.43788/0.14703/0.00644/0.42344, while comparator values and rankings remain unchanged. Tables 2–3 also revise TCP-Diffusion scores. Numerous new runtime, FuXi, spectral, lead-time, stochastic-sample, and cyclone-stratified results substantially expand the evidence. Changed sampling limits direct performance comparisons between versions.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies beta_s = 1 - cos(pi*s/(N-1)) and sigma_s = sqrt(beta_s), where v1 left these generic. This is a limited mathematical specification; as written, the schedule exceeds the stated beta_s range of (0,1). The principal equations remain unchanged, including Equations 12–14 moved to Appendix B.3. Appendix C explains existing metrics without adding theoretical results.

C1.justification: The principal contributions remain global TC rainfall forecasting, ARP-based change awareness, multimodal conditioning with NWP information, and claimed superiority over competing forecasts. v2 explicitly describes forecasting around an existing TC or given track location, consistent with v1's TC-centered task definition.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for Persistence's strength under a moving TC-centered window, interprets spectral agreement as capturing TC-scale structure, and attributes weaker phase/intensity performance to irregular cloud structures and rainfall-intensity variability. It also discusses stochastic samples as forecast uncertainty, hypothesizes why FuXi struggles, and qualifies usefulness when NWP forecast inputs are unavailable.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C supply detailed variable and pressure-level lists, split-selection information, denoising steps N=200, network depth K=4, noise settings, hardware/software versions, timing, and metric calculations. v2 states that code has been released at a repository, replacing v1's future-release promise; the earlier data-release commitment is absent. These are documentation and access-information changes, without evidence that existing training settings changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds context from diffusion-based climate emulation, TC forecasting, FuXi, and residual prediction in global weather models, including Price, Nguyen, Oskarsson, and Hu. It removes the Hersbach ERA5 reference. These additions refine the surrounding literature while retaining the original central novelty positioning.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes existing material: model design precedes dataset discussion, detailed data descriptions and 3DUNet equations move into appendices, and evaluation methods and results receive separate sections. The abstract and introduction are revised, training/inference pseudocode is added, and structured appendices integrate technical explanations and extended analyses.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands into a fixed-versus-moving forecast-window explanation, and Figure 2 is redrawn with explicit denoising, network, and reconstruction panels. New input visualizations, spectral and lead-time plots, sample grids, case comparisons, and Tables 4–8 substantially expand the visual presentation. Table 2 gains an ERA5-IFS row, and the document adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses the supplied v1's limited implementation documentation, absent dispersion reporting, and narrow diagnostic analysis. Appendices A–D and the added comparisons make the method easier to assess and reveal performance weaknesses across cyclone phases and intensities. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including the newly specified noise schedule's conflict with the stated variance range, which limits direct reproducibility.
